The `epidist` package enables users to estimate delay distributions while accounting for common reporting biases.
This vignette first introduces the background [@park2024estimating] required to understand the models implemented in `epidist`.
It then goes on to explain each model in turn.

# Background {#maths}

Estimating a delay distribution may appear to be simple: one could imagine fitting a probability distribution to a set of observed delays.
However, observed delays are often biased during an ongoing outbreak.
We begin by presenting a formalism for characterizing delay distributions as well as two main biases (truncation and censoring) affecting them.
We then present statistical models for correcting for these biases.

Any epidemiological delay requires a primary (starting) and a secondary (ending) event.
For example, the incubation period measures the time between infection (primary event) and symptom onset (secondary event).
Here, we use $p$ to denote the time of the primary event, and $s$ to denote the time of the secondary event.

## Forwards and backwards distributions

We can measure any delay distribution in two different ways.
First, we can measure the forward distribution $f_p(\tau)$, starting from a cohort of individuals who experienced the primary event at the same time $p$ and looking at when they experienced their secondary event.
Second, we can measure the backward distribution $b_s(\tau)$, starting from a cohort of individuals who experienced the secondary event at the same time $s$ and looking at when they experienced their primary event.
While the length of each individual delay $\tau = p-s$ remains constant whether we look at it forward or backwards, the shape of the distribution is affected by the differences in perspectives due to the differences in cohort composition.

To illustrate their differences, let's assume that primary and secondary events occur at rates, or equivalently incidences, $\mathcal{P}(p)$ and $\mathcal{S}(s)$, respectively.
Then, the total density $\mathcal{T}(p, s)$ of individuals with a primary event at time $p$ and secondary event at time $s$ can be expressed equivalently in terms of both forward and backward distributions:
$$
\mathcal{T}(p, s) = \mathcal{P}(p) f_p(s - p)  = \mathcal{S}(s) b_s(s - p).  (\#eq:forwards-backwards)
$$
Rearranging Equation \@ref(eq:forwards-backwards) gives
$$
b_s(\tau) = \frac{\mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau)}{\mathcal{S}(s)}. (\#eq:forwards-backwards2)
$$
The denominator of Equation \@ref(eq:forwards-backwards2), which corresponds to the incidence of secondary events, may be expressed as the integral over all possible delays
$$
\mathcal{S}(s) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau) \text{d} \tau,
$$
such that
$$
b_s(\tau) = \frac{\mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau)}{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathcal{P}(s - \tau) f_{s - \tau}(\tau) \text{d} \tau}.
$$
Here, we see that $b_s(\tau)$ depends not only on $f_{s - \tau}(\tau)$ but also on $\mathcal{P}(s - \tau)$, meaning that past changes in the incidence pattern will affect the shape of the distribution.
Particularly, when an epidemic is growing, we are more likely to observe shorter delays, causing an underestimation of the mean delay.
Therefore, we always want to characterize epidemiological delays from the forward perspective and estimate the forward distribution.
For this reason, our current methodology focuses on biases that affect the estimation of the forward distribution.

## Right truncation

One key bias that affects the forward distribution is right truncation.
Right truncation refers to the bias arising from the inability to observe future events and occurs when we observe data based on the secondary events.
For example, assume the data are right truncated and we don't observe secondary events past time $T$.
Then, we will only observe delays whose secondary events occurred before time $T$, causing us to underestimate the mean of the distribution as these delays will on average be shorter.

Bias from right truncation is greater when events are more likely to be more recent.
A common example of severely right truncated data is data collected during outbreaks when growth in incidence is exponential (so you are much more likely to have a recent event).
On the other hand, if data collection is continued until the end of an outbreak then many fewer events are likely to be more recent and so there will be little right truncation in general.

Mathematically right truncation can be described as follows.
Let $P$ and $S$ be random variables.
Let $F_p$ be the forward cumulative distribution.
Then, the probability of observing a delay of length $\tau$ given that the primary event occurred at time $p$ and a truncation at time $T$ can be written as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau \, | \, P = p, S < T) &= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau, P = p, S < T)}{\mathbb{P}(P = p, S < T)} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau < T \, | \, P = p)\mathbb{P}(P = p)}{\mathbb{P}(S < T \, | \, P = p)\mathbb{P}(P = p)} \\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(S = P + \tau < T \, | \, P = p)}{\mathbb{P}(S < T \, | \, P = p)} \\
&= \frac{f_p(\tau)}{\int_0^{T - p} f_p(x) \text{d}x} = \frac{f_p(\tau)}{F_p(T - p)}, \quad p + \tau < T.
\end{aligned}
$$

Examining this equation illustrates that (right) truncation renormalises the density by the values which are possible.
For example, if the distribution $x \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1)$ were right truncated by $T = 0.5$ then $x \sim \text{Unif}(0, 0.5)$.

## Interval censoring

The exact timing of epidemiological events is often unknown.
Instead, we may only know that the event happened within a certain interval.
We refer to this as interval censoring.
A very common example of interval censoring in epidemiology is date censoring, where we only know, or are using, data to the day of an event rather than the precise time.
Other forms of interval censoring, like weekly or monthly interval censoring, are also common.
When both primary and secondary events are interval censored, this is referred to as double censoring.

Mathematically single interval censoring is defined as follows.
Assume the secondary event $S$ is censored and so we don't know when the event exactly happened.
Instead, we only know that the secondary event happened between $S_L$ and $S_R$.
Then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P = p) &= \int_{S_L}^{S_R} f_p(y-p) dy\\
&= F_p(S_R-p) - F_p(S_L-p)
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, double interval censoring is defined as follows.
Now, assume that both the primary $P$ and secondary $S$ events are truncated.
We only know that the primary event happened between $P_L$ and $P_R$ and the secondary event happened between $S_L$ and $S_R$.
We now write $g_P$ to denote the unconditional distribution of primary events.
Then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R) &= \mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R)\\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R)}{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R)}\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z)\, dz  }\\
&= \int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x\,|\,P_L,P_R) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx
\end{aligned}
$$
where $g_P(x\,|\,P_L,P_R)$ represents the conditional distribution of primary event given lower $P_L$ and upper $P_R$ bounds.

# The naive model

The simplest approach to modelling epidemiological delay distributions is ignoring truncation and censoring biases and simply treating the delays as continuous fully observed data.
Then, the likelihood of observing a delay $\mathbf{Y}_i$ given parameter $\mathbf{\theta}$ is straightforward:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y}_i \, | \, \mathbf{\theta}) = f(y_i - x_i).
$$
where $y_i$ and $x_i$ are the observed primary and secondary event times.

As shown in [@park2024estimating]  when the data is double censored this modelling approach biases the mean by approximately a day as well as the standard deviation.
Where right truncation is also present biases can be more severe with plausible simulated scenarios leading to biased means that were >30% shorter than the true distributions.

# The latent model

This approach aims to account for the right truncation and double censoring using a generative modelling approach.
For each event, a latent variable is used to represent the exact time of the event.
This then allows the modelling of the continuous distribution, adjusted for the right truncation.
Whilst this is an approximation [@park2024estimating] showed good recovery of simulated distributions in a range of settings.
However, the use of two latent variables per observed delay means that this approach may scale poorly with larger datasets.
That being said this approach has been used successfully in multiple real-world outbreak settings ([@ward2022transmission]).
If using the latent model, please cite @park2024estimating in addition to `epidist`.

Mathematically this model is described as follows.
We look at the conditional probability that the secondary event $S$ falls between $S_L$ and $S_R$, given that the primary event $P$ falls between $P_L$ and $P_R$ and that the secondary event $S$ occurs before the truncation time $T$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \, | \, P_L < P < P_R, S<T)\\
&= \mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R, S<T \, | \, P_L < P < P_R, S<T)\\
&= \frac{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S_L < S < S_R, S<T)}{\mathbb{P}(P_L < P < P_R, S<T)}\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{z}^T g_P(z) f_z(w-z) \, dz \,dw  }\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z) F_z(T-z) \,dw  }\\
&= \frac{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} \int_{S_L}^{S_R} g_P(x|P_L, P_R) f_x(y-x) \,dy\, dx}{\int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(z|P_L, P_R) F_z(T-z) \,dw  }\\
\end{aligned}
$$
Using latent variables, we can now rewrite the observation likelihood as:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_i &\sim g_P(x_i \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i}) \\
y_i &\sim \text{Unif}(s_{L, i}, s_{R, i}) \\
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y} \, | \, \mathbf{\theta}) &= \prod_i \left[ \frac{f_{x_i}(y_i - x_i)}{\int_{P_{L, i}}^{P_{R, i}} g_P(z \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i}) F_z(T - z) \text{d}z} \right].
\end{aligned}
$$
As before, $g_P(z \, | \, p_{L, i}, p_{R, i})$ represents the conditional distribution of the primary event given lower $P_L$ and upper $P_R$ bounds; this is equivalent to modelling the incidence in primary events.

## Bounding the latent primary event time {#latent-bound}

`epidist` samples both latent offsets on the unit scale.
Write $w_{P, i} = p_{R, i} - p_{L, i}$ and $w_{S, i} = s_{R, i} - s_{L, i}$ for the two censoring window widths.
Then
$$
\tilde{p}_i \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1), \qquad
\tilde{s}_i \sim \text{Unif}(0, 1), \qquad
s_i = w_{S, i}\, \tilde{s}_i,
$$
and the primary event offset is ordinarily
$$
p_i = w_{P, i}\, \tilde{p}_i .
$$

When the two censoring windows overlap the delay must still be non-negative.
The primary event therefore has to precede the sampled secondary event.
The offset is then bounded by the sampled secondary offset rather than by the window width.
$$
p_i = s_i\, \tilde{p}_i .
$$

That upper bound is itself a parameter.
The map $\tilde{p}_i \mapsto p_i$ therefore has Jacobian determinant
$$
\left| \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial \tilde{p}_i} \right| = s_i ,
$$
Stan does not add this term for a transformation written this way.
See the [Stan user's guide on changes of variables](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/reparameterization.html#changes-of-variables).
The log density of these observations needs it explicitly.
$$
\log \mathcal{L}_i \;\longmapsto\; \log \mathcal{L}_i + \log s_i .
$$
The non-overlapping case needs no such term because $w_{P, i}$ is data, so its Jacobian is a constant that cancels.
The primary event density is used unnormalised here.
A constant normalising it over $[0, s_i]$ would itself depend on $s_i$.

The latent model formulation follows @ward2022transmission.
The need for this adjustment was identified in @bdbvlinelist and derived in @brand2026scalable.

# The marginal model

The marginal model corrects for the same biases as the latent model but integrates out the exact event times numerically, or analytically where closed-form solutions exist, rather than sampling latent variables.
This approach uses the primary event censored distribution implemented in the [`primarycensored`](https://primarycensored.epinowcast.org/) package [@primarycensored].
If using the marginal model, please cite `primarycensored` in addition to `epidist`.

Under the assumption that the forward distribution does not change within the censoring interval (i.e. $f_x = f$ for $x \in [P_L, P_R]$), the double censoring probability from Section \@ref(interval-censoring) simplifies to
$$
\mathbb{P}(S_L < S < S_R \mid P_L < P < P_R) = \int_{P_L}^{P_R} g_P(x \mid P_L, P_R) \left[F(S_R - x) - F(S_L - x)\right] \text{d}x.
$$
For common delay and primary event distributions, such as gamma or lognormal delays with uniform primary events, `primarycensored` provides closed-form analytical solutions to this integral.
For other combinations, numerical integration is used.

Right truncation at time $T$ is handled by normalising the likelihood as in the latent model:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{Y} \mid \mathbf{\theta}) = \prod_i \frac{\mathbb{P}(S_{L,i} < S_i < S_{R,i} \mid P_{L,i} < P_i < P_{R,i})}{\int_{P_{L,i}}^{P_{R,i}} g_P(z \mid p_{L,i}, p_{R,i}) F(T - z) \, \text{d}z}.
$$

Removing the latent variables reduces the number of parameters that must be sampled, and where analytical solutions exist the likelihood can be evaluated without numerical integration.
In addition, identical observations can be aggregated and the likelihood computed once per unique combination of delay, censoring windows, and covariates.
Together these make the marginal model substantially more efficient than the latent model, particularly for larger datasets with daily-censored data where many observations share the same structure.

For the mathematical details of primary event censored distributions, including the survival function derivation and closed-form solutions for specific distributions, see `vignette("why-it-works", package = "primarycensored")` and `vignette("analytic-solutions", package = "primarycensored")`.

# The meta model

The naive, latent and marginal models above all fit directly to individual delay observations.
Published estimates of a delay distribution are usually reported as summary statistics rather than individual observations, and the study's own estimation procedure is itself a source of bias [@charniga2024best; @park2024estimating].
The meta model lets `epidist` fit a single delay distribution to a mix of individual level data and published summary estimates.
Individual level rows use the marginal model likelihood of Section \@ref(the-marginal-model) unchanged, applied to `delay_lwr`, `delay_upr`, `pwindow`, `swindow` and `relative_obs_time`.
Each summary row is instead forward modelled: given the true continuous delay distribution, the model works out what the study's own estimation procedure would have converged to, and fits the reported value to that biased estimand with sampling uncertainty derived from the study sample size.
This means summaries that did not adjust for right truncation, or that treated interval censored data as continuous, still contribute unbiased information about the underlying distribution.
Study level heterogeneity, for example `mu ~ 1 + (1 | study)`, is specified through the `brms` formula rather than through the likelihood, exactly as for the other models above.
If using the meta model, please cite `primarycensored` in addition to `epidist`.
The meta model is experimental and its interface may still change.

## What we need from each study

Forward modelling a published estimate requires knowing something about how the study produced it.
We deliberately support only a few common cases rather than trying to encode every possible estimation procedure.
For each summary we need:

* **Roughly how it adjusted for interval censoring**, one of: no adjustment (it summarised integer date differences directly, the most common case in the literature), full adjustment (it used a latent variable or double interval censored likelihood targeting the continuous distribution), the uniform single interval approximation (it adjusted the secondary interval assuming a uniform delay within it, but left the primary interval uncorrected), or midpoint imputation (it assigned each delay to the centre of the interval it was observed in).
  These codes are a taxonomy of the common mistakes made when summarising interval censored delays rather than a closed set, and each is a forward model of one mistake, so a further mistake can be added as a further code.
* **Whether it adjusted for right truncation**, and if it did not, **the observation time** and **how collection stopped**.
  A cohort followed every primary event for the same observation time, so the observation time is the truncation point on the delay scale, that is how long after the primary events the data were extracted.
  A study that accrued primary events and stopped at a calendar date instead observed a given delay only for the primary events that occurred at least that long before the stop, and its observation time is the length of the collection window, which is usually easier to read off a paper.
* **The censoring windows**, the width of the interval each event was observed in, for example 1 for daily reporting or 7 for weekly reporting.
* **The sample size**, the number of delays the summary was computed from, or a reported standard error in its place, or a covariance matrix over the summaries it reported.
* **The smallest delay it counted**, where the study dropped delays below some point, so that its summaries describe a left truncated delay distribution.

Systematic reviews rarely record all of this study metadata.
Where a review does not report how a study adjusted for these biases, an assumption must be made and stated explicitly alongside any results; ideally reviews would report this metadata directly so that this judgement is not left to whoever reuses the estimates.
The reporting checklist of @charniga2024best covers exactly this metadata.
If studies and systematic reviews adopted it, fitting to published estimates in this way would become easier and more routine.

## The biased estimand

For a summary row, let $f(\tau; \theta)$ and $F(\tau; \theta)$ be the forward density and distribution function of the delay of Section \@ref(maths), and let $g_p$ be the distribution of a primary event within its censoring window of width $w_p$: uniform when incidence was constant over the study period, or weighted towards more recent times by an exponential growth rate when it was not.
Write
$$
F_{pc}(\tau; \theta) = \mathbb{P}(\tau^\star + U \le \tau), \quad \tau^\star \sim f(\cdot \, ; \theta), \; U \sim g_p,
$$
for the distribution function of the delay plus an independent primary event offset, which `primarycensored` provides.
One forward model is used per censoring adjustment code, each right truncated at the study's grid cutoff $D$ (its observation time if it did not adjust for right truncation, otherwise a user set `max_delay`) unless the study adjusted for right truncation itself.

A study with **no censoring adjustment** summarised integer date differences directly, observing the discrete double censored delay
$$
q_j = \frac{F_{pc}(j w_s; \theta) - F_{pc}((j-1) w_s; \theta)}{F_{pc}(w_s \lfloor D / w_s \rfloor; \theta)}, \quad j = 1, \dots, \lfloor D / w_s \rfloor, (\#eq:meta-grid)
$$
where $w_s$ is the secondary censoring window and bin $j$ carries the delay value $(j-1) w_s$; the truncation point is discretised to the last full grid boundary $w_s \lfloor D / w_s \rfloor$.
The implied mean, variance and kurtosis follow by summing over this grid.

A study with **full adjustment** reported the moments of $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$ itself, right truncated at $D$ when it did not separately adjust for truncation:
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tau^k \mid \tau \le D] = \frac{\int_0^D k t^{k-1} \left(F(D; \theta) - F(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}{F(D; \theta)}, \quad k = 1, \dots, 4. (\#eq:meta-trunc-moments)
$$
When the study also adjusted for right truncation this reduces to the ordinary family moments used by `add_mean_sd()`.

A study using the **uniform single interval approximation** left the primary interval uncorrected, so it effectively observed $\tau^\star + U$.
Its implied moments are the raw moments of $F_{pc}$, right truncated at $D$ when the study did not separately adjust for truncation:
$$
\mathbb{E}[(\tau^\star + U)^k \mid \tau^\star + U \le D] =
\frac{\int_0^D k t^{k-1} \left(F_{pc}(D; \theta) - F_{pc}(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}{F_{pc}(D; \theta)},
\quad k = 1, \dots, 4. (\#eq:meta-uniform-moments)
$$
Equation \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) is evaluated by Simpson's rule over the delay distribution function, and Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) by Simpson's rule over $F_{pc}$.
Where the study also adjusted for right truncation and the primary event distribution is uniform, the convolution is instead exact:
$$
\mu_{pc} = \mu + \frac{w_p}{2}, \quad
\sigma_{pc}^2 = \sigma^2 + \frac{w_p^2}{12}, \quad
\mu_{4,pc} = \mu_4 + 6 \sigma^2 \frac{w_p^2}{12} + \frac{w_p^4}{80}, (\#eq:meta-uniform-exact)
$$
where $\mu$, $\sigma^2$ and $\mu_4$ are the mean, variance and fourth central moment of $f(\cdot \, ; \theta)$.

A study using **midpoint imputation** assigned each delay to the centre of the interval it was observed in, so it summarised the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) with bin $j$ carrying the delay value $(j - 1/2) w_s$ rather than $(j-1) w_s$.
Its implied mean is therefore the grid mean plus $w_s / 2$, every central moment is unchanged, and its distribution function is the grid one evaluated at $y - w_s / 2$.

## Accrual truncation

The truncation above conditions on the delay falling below a single cutoff, which is what a cohort followed for a common observation time gives.
A study that accrued primary events over a window and stopped collecting at its calendar end instead saw a delay of $d$ only for the primary events that occurred at least $d$ before the stop.
With primary events arriving at a rate proportional to $\exp(r t)$ over a window of length $A$, the amount of such follow up is
$$
w(d) = \int_0^{A - d} \exp(r t) \, \text{d}t = \frac{\exp(r (A - d)) - 1}{r}, \quad 0 \le d \le A, (\#eq:meta-accrual)
$$
which tends to $A - d$ as $r$ tends to zero.
This is the dynamical bias of @park2024estimating; for a long window and a growing epidemic it approaches an exponential tilt of the delay distribution by $\exp(-r d)$.
The estimand is then $f(d; \theta) w(d)$ renormalised over $[0, A]$, with $A$ taken from `relative_obs_time`, so for an accrual study that field is the length of the collection window rather than a cohort cutoff.
In practice the weight is applied to the cell masses of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) at each bin's delay value, and to the quadrature used for Equations \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) and \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) at each node's midpoint, renormalising in both cases.
Equation \@ref(eq:meta-accrual) is the smooth average of the follow up actually available, which is a step function of the primary event's censoring window.
It is exact for a study that adjusted for censoring, where $d$ is the underlying delay, and exact on the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) when $w_p = w_s$ and both divide $A$, because the calendar stop and the date differencing then discretise together.
For Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) the weighted quantity is $\tau^\star + U$ rather than the time from the primary event's window, so $w$ is evaluated at $d - w_p / 2$ to average the primary offset back out.
The weight applies only to studies that did not adjust for right truncation, because a study that did has already removed it.

## Sampling likelihoods

With study sample size $n$ and reported value $y$, and writing $m_1$, $\sigma$ and $\kappa$ for the mean, standard deviation and kurtosis (the fourth central moment divided by $\sigma^4$) implied by the forward model above, a **reported mean** is given a normal sampling distribution
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(m_1, \; \text{se}_{m_1} \right), (\#eq:meta-mean-lik)
$$
where $\text{se}_{m_1}$ is the standard error reported by the study when one was given, and $\sigma / \sqrt{n}$ otherwise.
A **reported standard deviation** is likewise given a normal sampling distribution, using the kurtosis based asymptotic standard error of a sample standard deviation
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(\sigma, \; \text{se}_\sigma \right), \quad
\text{se}_\sigma = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\kappa - 1}{4 n}}. (\#eq:meta-sd-lik)
$$
The normal theory expression $\sigma / \sqrt{2(n-1)}$ is not used because it assumes the estimand itself is normally distributed and is two to four times too narrow for the right skewed distributions delays usually follow.

A **reported quantile** at probability $p$ is fitted on the cumulative probability scale, which avoids inverting the distribution function of the biased estimand:
$$
p \sim \text{Normal}\left(G(y), \; \text{se}_p\right), (\#eq:meta-quantile-lik)
$$
where $G$ is the distribution function implied by the forward model for the row's censoring adjustment, and $\text{se}_p$ is the binomial standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ of an empirical distribution function.
Studies report a quantile's uncertainty on the delay scale, so a standard error $\text{se}_y$ supplied for a quantile row is taken on that scale and converted by the delta method,
$$
\text{se}_p = g(y) \, \text{se}_y, (\#eq:meta-quantile-se)
$$
where $g$ is the density of the biased estimand at the reported value: the mass of the grid cell $y$ falls in divided by $w_s$ for a discrete estimand, which is the slope of the continuity corrected $G$ there, and the derivative of $G$ otherwise.
The converted standard error is held away from zero so that a quantile reported far into the tail cannot give a degenerate likelihood.
For the discretely summarised case $G$ is continuity corrected by interpolating the grid distribution function linearly through the mid points of its cells, because a reported quantile of day resolution data otherwise always lands on a jump of the step function.

## Summaries from the same study

Summaries that one study computed from the same delays are correlated, so they are fitted jointly.
Two summaries are fitted together when they agree on every field other than the summary itself, that is on the study, its metadata, and any covariates supplied, so a linear predictor built from those fields cannot vary within a group.
A summary supplied with its own standard error is fitted on its own, because that standard error replaces the sampling uncertainty the joint likelihood would derive.

A **mean and a standard deviation** from one study are given the asymptotic bivariate normal of the pair
$$
\begin{pmatrix} y_{m} \\ y_{\sigma} \end{pmatrix} \sim
\text{Normal}\left(
\begin{pmatrix} m_1 \\ \sigma \end{pmatrix}, \;
\frac{1}{n}\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma^2 & \mu_3 / (2 \sigma) \\
\mu_3 / (2 \sigma) & \sigma^2 (\kappa - 1) / 4
\end{pmatrix}
\right), (\#eq:meta-moment-pair)
$$
where $\mu_3$ is the third central moment of the implied estimand.
The off diagonal is $\text{Cov}(\bar{x}, s^2) = \mu_3 / n$ carried onto the standard deviation scale by the delta method.
The implied correlation is $\gamma_1 / \sqrt{\kappa - 1}$, with $\gamma_1 = \mu_3 / \sigma^3$ the skewness, and $\kappa \ge \gamma_1^2 + 1$ holds for every distribution, so the covariance matrix is positive definite.
Moments taken from the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) or from quadrature can sit a little outside that bound, so the correlation is held strictly inside $[-1, 1]$.

**Several quantiles** from one study at probabilities $p_1 < \dots < p_k$ with values $y_1 < \dots < y_k$ cut the delay axis into $k+1$ cells, and the number of delays falling in each is multinomial
$$
(c_1, \dots, c_{k+1}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(n, \; \left(G(y_1), \; G(y_2) - G(y_1), \; \dots, \; 1 - G(y_k)\right)\right), (\#eq:meta-quantile-set)
$$
with $c_j = \text{round}(n p_j) - \text{round}(n p_{j-1})$ and $c_{k+1} = n - \text{round}(n p_k)$.
Rounding the cumulative probabilities rather than the increments keeps every count non negative and makes them sum to $n$.
A single reported quantile reduces Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set) to the binomial, of which Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-lik) is the normal approximation, so quantile rows use Equation \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set) unless the study supplied its own standard error.
A cell whose implied probability is zero while the study saw delays in it gives a log likelihood of $-\infty$.

Summaries of different kinds from the same study, such as a mean and a median, are still treated as independent given the parameters.
This understates their joint uncertainty and is a documented approximation of the meta model, alongside the normal approximations above degrading for small study sample sizes.

## A reported covariance matrix

A study that cannot share its delays can report the vector of summaries it computed together with the covariance matrix between them, which it can estimate from its own delays by bootstrap.
This is the reporting format we recommend, because it carries the correlation between the reported quantities rather than throwing it away.
Writing $y$ for the reported vector and $\Sigma$ for the supplied matrix,
$$
y \sim \text{Normal}\left(m(\theta), \; \Sigma\right), (\#eq:meta-mvn)
$$
where $m(\theta)$ holds the implied summary for each reported quantity, that is $m_1$ for a mean, $\sigma$ for a standard deviation, and the implied quantile at $p$ for a quantile.
This generalises Equations \@ref(eq:meta-moment-pair) and \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set), which derive the covariance from the sample size and the implied moments.
Here it is supplied instead, so a mixture of summary types no longer has to be treated as independent.
The Cholesky factor of $\Sigma$ is taken once when the model data are built rather than inside the sampler.

A quantile reported this way is on the delay scale, so $m$ needs the inverse of $G$, which has no closed form on the discrete grid.
It is read off by inverse linear interpolation between the two points of $G$ that bracket $p$, on the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid) for a discrete estimand and on the quadrature grid otherwise.
That keeps the implied quantile a differentiable function of $\theta$, which a root search would not, at the cost of the curvature of $G$ over one cell.

## Left truncation

A study that only counted delays of at least $L$ reported summaries of a left truncated estimand, so every quantity above is conditioned on $\tau > L$.
This generalises the expressions rather than replacing them, and each reduces to the form already given when $L = 0$.

On the grid of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-grid), the cells recording a delay below $L$ are dropped and the rest renormalised by the mass they hold, which is $F_{pc}(D) - F_{pc}(L)$ whenever $L$ falls on a grid boundary.
The truncated moments of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-trunc-moments) pick up a boundary term,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\tau^k \mid L < \tau \le D] =
\frac{L^k \left(F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)\right) +
\int_L^D k t^{k-1} \left(F(D; \theta) - F(t; \theta)\right) \text{d}t}
{F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}, \quad k = 1, \dots, 4, (\#eq:meta-left-moments)
$$
and the same applies to Equation \@ref(eq:meta-uniform-moments) with $F_{pc}$ in place of $F$.
The distribution function used for quantile rows becomes
$$
G(y) = \frac{F(y; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}{F(D; \theta) - F(L; \theta)}, \quad L < y \le D, (\#eq:meta-left-cdf)
$$
zero at or below $L$ and one above $D$, with $F(D; \theta)$ replaced by one for a study that adjusted for right truncation itself.
The accrual weight of Equation \@ref(eq:meta-accrual) is unchanged, because it multiplies the same cells and nodes, which now start at $L$.
Individual level rows pass $L$ to `primarycensored` as their left truncation point, exactly as the marginal model does.

## Meta-analysis standards

The meta model follows some standard meta-analytic practice and departs from other parts of it deliberately.
Both are stated explicitly here rather than left implicit.

Sampling uncertainty for every summary type is approximated by a normal distribution, with the standard errors of Equations \@ref(eq:meta-mean-lik) to \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-se) used when a study does not report one directly.
This is standard inverse variance meta-analysis practice, and it degrades for small study sample sizes, where the normal approximation to a mean, standard deviation or quantile is least accurate.

Study level heterogeneity is pooled through the `brms` formula, following standard random effects meta-analysis practice, for example `mu ~ 1 + (1 | study)`.
This extends to any distributional parameter, not only the mean.
`sigma ~ 1 + (1 | study)` places a random effect on the standard deviation dpar in the same way, so heterogeneity in spread across studies is pooled as well as heterogeneity in location.

Reported medians and interquartile ranges are modelled directly as quantile rows, rather than converted to a mean and standard deviation before fitting.
Converting a median and interquartile range to a mean and standard deviation assumes the underlying distribution is symmetric, which delay distributions rarely are, so modelling them directly avoids introducing that bias.

Summaries reported from the same delays are fitted jointly through Equations \@ref(eq:meta-moment-pair) and \@ref(eq:meta-quantile-set), rather than as separate terms.
Without this a study reporting a median with an interquartile range would contribute three near independent terms for one set of delays, and so be over-weighted relative to a study reporting a mean and a standard deviation.
What remains approximate is the correlation between summaries of different kinds, such as a mean and a median from the same study.

Finally, `loo` and other information criteria compare log likelihoods, and what one observation contributes to that sum differs between an individual level row and a summary row.
An observation is also a group of summaries rather than a single reported value, in the same way that one row of aggregated data stands for many individual delays.
`loo` is only meaningful for comparing two meta model fits applied to the same mix of individual and summary data.
Comparing `loo` across fits with different data included, whether different studies or a different mix of individual and summary rows, is not meaningful.
